Love vast.ai, but wishes it were easier to work with persistent disks over time; now only uses it for one-off expensive jobs.

Tried it in 2018: compute prices were competitive, but most instances had lousy bandwidth. Staff were friendly and helpful. In 2020, years after last renting anything, they tried to charge their expired card $1.70 and only explained it with "that's weird".

Potential user likes the idea but dislikes how many clicks it takes to find even an approximate price. Others said the marketplace/pricing page loads very slowly on first visit, with no in-page loading indicator.
Would-be host says the Ubuntu requirement means they can't contribute their compute, and neither can Windows gamers or users of other distros.

Commenter says running untrusted code from renters, even inside a container, is a terrible idea for hosts because of container escapes and the legal risk of strangers using your network. They wouldn't host unless using a VM with PCIe passthrough and VPN-tunneled traffic.

Commenter sees the platform as a no-go for training on private data, or even privately labeled public images, on strangers' machines. They are also skeptical of promised encrypted environments given SGX exploits.
Renters get a full Linux shell and can deploy images, including some with hashcat preinstalled.

As a renter, found vast.ai pretty unreliable: hosts, bandwidth and performance were all over the place versus what the console lists (suspects benchmark gaming). Even on-demand instances fall well short of the reported reliability/uptime metrics.
The software stack is decent but still a pain to use, with significant limitations and hoops to jump through compared to a GCP/AWS GPU instance.

Host economics critique: median US verified RTX 3090 rents for $0.38/hr. After vast's 25% cut, power and taxes, a host nets about $0.20/hr, a ~14-month ROI at full use. A100 PCIe at a $0.79/hr median on a $15k card would never pay off.
After frustrating experiences with AWS, Azure and GCP, the poster found Vast.ai "a breath of fresh air" for running hashcat in the cloud.
User reported finding a Chinese host on vast.ai masquerading as a US host, raising concerns about the accuracy of host location listings.
